title: The Educated Barbarian: Meditations analysis (part. 1)
summary: NH launches the Stoicism cycle of The Educated Barbarian, reading Marcus Aurelius, then Epictetus, Seneca and the Discourses, with nihilism to follow. He reads Marcus's values from Book 1 and discusses Book 2 on dealing with difficult people, God as nature or the universe, the self-sufficiency of the self, and gradations of sin. He argues kindness only has value when a man is capable of being dangerous.
claims: The Stoicism reading order: Meditations, Enchiridion, Seneca's On the Happy Life, Epictetus' Discourses, likely a year at one episode a week; nihilism comes next
Stoicism is the philosophy he most identifies with in how he lives day to day
Subscribing to only one way of thinking makes you miss much wisdom; embrace several doctrines
Read the book yourself before hearing his take so it doesn't taint your understanding
Marcus saw lacking talent for rhetoric and poetry as a blessing, like the Hagakure
Meet meddlers and the envious with kindness; answering them with their own methods makes you no better than them
In the Meditations, God means the creator or universe (Jupiter/Zeus), not the Abrahamic God
Imagination in Stoicism means passions and interpretations not based on what's happening now, i.e. outside your control
Stoicism holds that the self is self-sufficient for happiness; wealth, fame and friends can't guarantee it and often separate you from the self
Time alone as a teen was how he discovered who he was; teens chasing others' approval learn others' minds more than their own and become unhappy
Nothing outside the self can harm or change the self; pressure to change comes from within
Sins from pleasure are worse than sins from passion or pain
Stoicism is judgmental, so you must exemplify it rather than just claim others are wrong
A Stoic is by definition virtuous; cold, unemotional people who use Stoic traits for evil fall outside Stoicism
Being a man requires being somewhat dangerous; kindness from someone incapable of harm is worthless, like a pet's or a child's
